newsitem.title: JAPAN: PM's remarks seen reviving Japan gold debate.
newsitem.headline: PM's remarks seen reviving Japan gold debate.

text.p: A remark by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto that Japan had in the past been tempted to sell U.S. Treasuries and boost its gold reserves will revive a controversial debate over the nation's gold policy, experts said on Tuesday.

On Monday, Hashimoto, responding to a question after a speech at Columbia University in New York, said: "Actually several times in the past, we have been tempted to sell large lots of U.S. Treasuries."
He said that in terms of fund management Japan had not taken "the most advantageous road", adding: "Rather we had the choice to sell Treasuries and increase our gold reserves."
He was answering a question on whether it was in Japan's long-term interests to continue to accumulate U.S. government securities.
As of the end of May, Japan's external reserves stood at about $221.761 billion, the Finance Ministry said.
Financial industry officials estimate that about 80 percent of Japan's external reserves is in U.S. dollars.
Japan's accumulated appraisal losses on its reserves reached 7.1603 trillion yen as of March 31, the end of the 1996/97 fiscal year, the Finance Ministry said.

Financial industry officials say the losses were partly caused by the dollar's steep fall following the 1985 Plaza Agreement by the Group of Five (G5) industrialised nations to promote depreciation of the dollar.
"Hashimoto's remark (on gold) will revive the long-running debate here," said Kyuya Shimazaki, a professor at Kanagawa University's economic department.
"Japan now depends excessively on U.S. securities and should consider diversifying the country's reserves. Gold is an option we can take," Shimazaki said.

International Monetary Fund data shows that Japan's gold reserves as of June 1996 were 754 tonnes, compared with the United States' 8,140 tonnes. France had 2,546 tonnes, Germany 2,960 tonnes and Italy 2,074 tonnes.
"It's clear that Japan's gold holdings are sharply lower than those of other industrialised nations," said Koichiro Kamei, a manager of the World Gold Council's Tokyo office.
"Hashimoto's comment is quite unusual. Making no comment on gold has been the Japanese government's policy, given the possible impact on the market," Kamei said.
Last month, a veteran Japanese legislator voiced concern about the risk of keeping a large proportion of the country's external reserves in dollars.
Masaaki Nakayama, a member of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party who serves on the Lower House of parliament's budget committee, told Reuters at that time that Japan should boost its gold holdings.
"Excessive dependence on the U.S. dollar and sharply smaller gold reserves are my growing concern," Nakayama said.
"Holding more gold should be considered."
Some experts are cautious, saying increasing gold reserves might trigger repercussions from the United States.

"Buying more gold for the external reserves could indicate less trust in the U.S. dollar. I'm not sure if the Japanese government can take such a brave move," said a gold industry expert who asked not to be named.

In a statement dated June 23 and released on Tuesday in Tokyo, the Finance Ministry said that the prime minister's intention was to maintain the consistent policy of the Japanese government, bearing in mind the good relations between Japan and the United States.

Spot gold prices were stable in Asia on Tuesday after Hashimoto's comments helped gold rise overnight in New York. By late afternoon, bullion was quoted at $339.15/65 per ounce, against $339.10/60 at the New York Monday closing and London's close at $338.00.
